lec06kp03-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p1-bridge.text: KP01 slid a small kernel over an image, multiplying and adding, to get a feature map. That is only part of a convolutional layer: what exactly happens inside one layer?

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p1|Three-stage flow: stage 1 convolution (the kernel slides and multiplies and adds, giving a feature map), stage 2 detector (an activation function on every cell), stage 3 pooling (one summary per block, smaller map); find-edges filter analogy: apply the filter, keep positive responses, shrink; the two questions of the unit.

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-18.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p1#18
lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-18.text: Prerequisites: kernel and feature map (KP01); activation functions (Week 2); backpropagation and gradient descent (Week 3).

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-19.name: term:convolution stage
lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-19.text:
The kernel slides over the input
and multiplies and adds at each
position, giving the feature map $s$.

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-21.name: term:detector stage
lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-21.text:
An activation function on every
cell decides how strongly that
position "lights up".

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-23.name: term:pooling stage

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-25.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p1#25
lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-25.text:
This unit answers two questions: what exactly happens inside one convolutional layer,
and where do the nine numbers of the kernel come from?

lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-26.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p1#26
lec06kp03-u01-p1-nf-lec06-kp03-p1-26.text: The sliding multiply-and-add of KP01 is only stage one; a full layer is convolution, detector, pooling.

lec06kp03-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p2-bridge.text: In the convolution stage the kernel slides over the input, like a "find edges" filter. Before deep learning, how did engineers design a kernel, and what do its numbers look like?

lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p2|Definition of an edge; horizontal Prewitt kernel rows [1,1,1], [0,0,0], [−1,−1,−1], top row minus bottom row; vertical Prewitt kernel rows [1,0,−1], [1,0,−1], [1,0,−1], left column minus right column; blue +1, red −1, grey 0.

lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-30.name: term:edge
lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-30.text:
Edge: a place in an image
where the brightness
changes suddenly.

lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-31.name: term:Prewitt kernel
lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-31.text:
Before deep learning became
popular, engineers designed
kernels by hand to find edges.
The classic pair: the $3\times3$
Prewitt kernels.

lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-45.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p2#45
lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-45.text:
largest on a horizontal edge,
bright and dark top vs bottom

lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-56.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p2#56
lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-56.text:
largest on a vertical edge,
bright and dark left vs right

lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-57.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p2#57
lec06kp03-u01-p2-nf-lec06-kp03-p2-57.text: The horizontal $K_{\mathrm h}$ finds top-bottom contrast, the vertical $K_{\mathrm v}$ left-right contrast.

lec06kp03-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec06kp03-u01-p3-title.text: A patch: minus six and zero

lec06kp03-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p3-bridge.text: Before deep learning, the two Prewitt kernels computed the top row minus the bottom row and the left column minus the right column. On a small patch, dark on top and bright below, what does each give?

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p3|Patch X rows [0,0,0], [1,1,1], [2,2,2], dark on top; horizontal kernel rows give 0, 0, −6, total −6; vertical kernel 0 per row, total 0; X transposed, dark on the left: horizontal 0, vertical −6; a red box marks a negative response; Added: a large absolute value means an edge, the sign tells which side is brighter.

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-13.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p3#13
lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-13.text: Kernel as large as the patch: one placement

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-49.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p3#49
lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-49.text:
$K_{\mathrm h}$: row $0$: $0\cdot1+0\cdot1+0\cdot1=0$
row $1$ is multiplied by $0$: $0$
row $2$: $2\cdot(-1)+2\cdot(-1)+2\cdot(-1)=-6$
total $-6$

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-50.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p3#50
lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-50.text:
$K_{\mathrm v}$: each row $1\cdot v+0\cdot v+(-1)\cdot v=0$
($v$ is the value of that row); total $0$

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-51.name: term:transpose
lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-51.text:
Transpose: rows and
columns swapped
→ dark on the left

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-80.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p3#80
lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-80.text:
Large absolute value: an edge in that direction. The sign: which side is
brighter; $K_{\mathrm h}$ is positive when the top is brighter, negative like $X$'s $-6$.

lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-81.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p3#81
lec06kp03-u01-p3-nf-lec06-kp03-p3-81.text: On $X$, dark above bright: $K_{\mathrm h}$ gives $-6$, $K_{\mathrm v}$ gives $0$; on its transpose they swap.

lec06kp03-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p4-bridge.text: On the patch the horizontal kernel gives minus six and the vertical one zero: one number per patch. What does a whole $6\times6$ image become after stage one?

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4|6×6 image, rows 1 to 3 and columns 0 to 3 of brightness 2 (orange), the rest 0; horizontal kernel valid output 6−3+1=4, 4×4 feature map rows [−6,−6,−4,−2], [0,0,0,0], [6,6,4,2], [6,6,4,2]; cells s[0,0]=−6 (top edge), s[2,0]=6 (bottom edge), s[0,3]=−2 (barely covered); row 1 windows have identical top and bottom rows, so 0.

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-128.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4#128
lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-128.text:
green: positive (bright above)
red: negative (dark above)

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-129.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4#129
lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-129.text:
$s[0,0]$: rows $0$–$2$. Top row all $0$, bottom all $2$:
$0-2\cdot3=-6$, the top edge, dark above bright.

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-130.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4#130
lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-130.text:
$s[2,0]$: rows $2$–$4$. Top row all $2$, bottom all $0$:
$2\cdot3-0=6$, the bottom edge, bright above dark.

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-131.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4#131
lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-131.text:
$s[0,3]$: columns $3$–$5$; only column $3$ of the bottom
row is $2$: $0-2=-2$, a small part, a smaller response.

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-132.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4#132
lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-132.text:
The windows of row $1$ cover rows $1$ to $3$,
whose top and bottom rows are identical: $0$.

lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-133.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p4#133
lec06kp03-u01-p4-nf-lec06-kp03-p4-133.text: Stage one: the top edge gives negatives, the bottom edge positives; a barely covered block gives less.

lec06kp03-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p5-bridge.text: Stage one gave signed edges: the top edge negative, $-6,-6,-4,-2$, the bottom edge positive. Stage two applies an activation to every cell: which numbers survive?

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5|Left: feature map s rows [−6,−6,−4,−2], [0,0,0,0], [6,6,4,2], [6,6,4,2]; through ReLU(a)=max(0,a); right: r rows [0,0,0,0], [0,0,0,0], [6,6,4,2], [6,6,4,2]; only the bottom edge stays; Added common error: size without sign, a dark-above-bright edge vanishes after the ReLU.

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-39.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5#39
lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-39.text: Detector: an activation on every cell

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-79.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5#79
lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-79.text:
The $-6,-6,-4,-2$ of row $0$ all become $0$, the rest stays:
only the bottom edge, bright above dark, is still lit.

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-82.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5#82
lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-82.text: Negatives become $0$, positives stay. Written out,

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-84.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5#84
lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-84.text: Common error: size only, no sign

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-85.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5#85
lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-85.text:
Looking only at the size of the output of $K_{\mathrm h}$
and forgetting its sign: an edge dark above bright
gives a negative number and vanishes after the ReLU.

lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-86.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p5#86
lec06kp03-u01-p5-nf-lec06-kp03-p5-86.text: The detector keeps only positive responses: the negative top edge becomes $0$, only the bottom edge stays.

lec06kp03-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p6-bridge.text: After the detector, $r$ keeps only the bottom edge, $6,6,4,2$, but it is still $4\times4$. How does stage three shrink it, and what does the result say?

lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p6|r rows [0,0,0,0], [0,0,0,0], [6,6,4,2], [6,6,4,2], cut by orange lines into four 2×2 blocks; max pooling keeps each maximum; y rows [0,0], [6,4]; bottom left 6,6,6,6 gives 6, bottom right 4,2,4,2 gives 4; 6×6 → 4×4 → 2×2; reading 6 and 4: the left half is entirely bottom edge, the right half only partly.

lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-55.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p6#55
lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-55.text: The top-left and top-right blocks are all $0$: row $0$ is $[0,0]$.

lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-57.name: term:max pooling
lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-57.text:
Max pooling: cut the map into non-overlapping
$2\times2$ blocks and keep each block's maximum.

lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-60.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p6#60

lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-61.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p6#61
lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-61.text: The $16$ numbers of $4\times4$ shrink to $4$ summaries.

lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-62.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p6#62
lec06kp03-u01-p6-nf-lec06-kp03-p6-62.text: Max pooling keeps each block's maximum: $y$ has rows $[0,0]$ and $[6,4]$; the bottom edge, fuller on the left.

lec06kp03-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p7-bridge.text: Max pooling keeps each block's maximum, and the three stages turned the $6\times6$ image into the $2\times2$ rows $[0,0]$ and $[6,4]$. What goes wrong if one stage is missing?

lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p7|Sizes: image 6×6 → convolution 4×4 → detector 4×4 → pooling 2×2; three cards: without the detector (stacked linear is still linear, two convolutions equal one), without pooling (map too large, small shifts matter more, approximate stability in KP08–KP09), without convolution (back to the fully connected layer, losing sparse connectivity and parameter sharing); common error: a convolutional layer is a single multiplication.

lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-25.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p7#25
lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-25.text:
Convolution is only multiply-and-
add, a linear operation. Stacked
linear operations are still one
(Week 2): two convolutions equal
one. The activation adds nonlinearity.

lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-26.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p7#26
lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-26.text:
The feature map is about as large
as the input, so later layers have
many numbers. Pooling shrinks it
and makes small shifts matter less,
only approximately (KP08–KP09).

lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-27.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p7#27
lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-27.text:
We are back to the fully connected
layer of KP01 and lose sparse
connectivity and parameter sharing.

lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-28.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p7#28
lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-28.text: Common error: thinking a convolutional layer is a single multiplication. It has three stages.

lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-29.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p7#29
lec06kp03-u01-p7-nf-lec06-kp03-p7-29.text: Each stage is needed: nonlinearity, a smaller map, and neighbours with one shared kernel.

lec06kp03-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p8-bridge.text: Each stage is needed, and the three stages turn an image into a small summary. But the horizontal kernel finds only top-bottom edges: for another task, telling cats from dogs, are these nine hand-set numbers still right?

lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p8|Left: the hand-set horizontal Prewitt kernel with fixed numbers; right: nine learnable weights K[0,0] to K[2,2]; forward (green): kernel → convolution → ReLU → pooling → later layers → loss e; backward (red): the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each K[m,n]; gradient descent: K[m,n] ← K[m,n] − η ∂e/∂K[m,n]; e is the loss, η the learning rate.

lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-65.name: term:learnable weight
lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-65.text:
Learnable weight: every number $K[m,n]$ of the kernel,
decided by the data like the weights of Week 2.

lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-66.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p8#66
lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-66.text:
Different tasks and data need different kernels: real images
have slanted lines, textures, corners and fur patterns, and
hand-tuning nine numbers for every case is not practical.

lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-77.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p8#77
lec06kp03-u01-p8-nf-lec06-kp03-p8-77.text: Kernel numbers are weights: forward to the loss $e$, back-propagate, update by gradient descent.

lec06kp03-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p9-bridge.text: Learn the kernel by backpropagation: gradient descent updates each $K[m,n]$ with the partial derivative of the loss. Convolution is a long chain of multiply-and-add: can this derivative be computed?

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p9|Left: the 6×6 image, green frame the window of s[2,0] (rows 2 to 4, columns 0 to 2), yellow box I[2,0]=2; right: Added, s[2,0]=I[2,0]K[0,0]+I[2,1]K[0,1]+…+I[4,2]K[2,2], ∂s[i,j]/∂K[m,n]=I[i+m,j+n], ∂s[2,0]/∂K[0,0]=I[2,0]=2; definition of a partial derivative; the chain rule adds up positions; learned kernels can catch textures; common error: only Prewitt kernels.

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-42.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p9#42
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-42.text: Convolution is linear in the kernel

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-86.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p9#86
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-86.text: Each $K[m,n]$ multiplies one pixel, so its partial derivative is that pixel:

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-89.name: term:partial derivative
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-89.text:
Partial derivative: the rate of change when only one variable moves (Week 3). The same
$K[m,n]$ is used at every position; backpropagation adds all contributions by the chain rule.

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-90.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p9#90
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-90.text:
A learned kernel may catch edges like Prewitt,
or textures, spots and more complex patterns:
backpropagation replaces hand-tuning.

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-91.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p9#91
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-91.text:
Common error: thinking a convolutional network
can only use edge kernels like Prewitt. It is an
example of hand-tuning; kernels are learned.

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-92.name: term:convolutional neural network
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-92.text:
Convolutional neural network:
built mainly from such layers

lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-93.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p9#93
lec06kp03-u01-p9-nf-lec06-kp03-p9-93.text: The gradient is easy: the partial derivative of $s[i,j]$ with respect to $K[m,n]$ is the pixel it multiplies, e.g. $I[2,0]=2$.

lec06kp03-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec06kp03-u01-p10-bridge.text: Convolution is linear in the kernel, so the partial derivative is the pixel it multiplies. In this unit the kernel is laid down as it is, giving the $-6$ of X: rotated half a turn first, would the response be the same?

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-1.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10|Added: horizontal kernel rows [1,1,1], [0,0,0], [−1,−1,−1], after 180° rows [−1,−1,−1], [0,0,0], [1,1,1], exactly its own negative; on X: original −6, rotated 6; two conventions: this unit lays it down as it is (as KP01), the textbook convolution rotates by 180° first; whether to flip and the exact formula: KP04.

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-54.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10#54
lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-54.text: after $180^\circ$ it is exactly $-$$K_{\mathrm h}$, its own negative

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-55.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10#55
lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-55.text:
On $X$: $K_{\mathrm h}$ gives $-6$, the rotated kernel gives $6$.
The response changes sign.

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-56.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10#56
lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-56.text:
This unit follows KP01: the kernel is laid down as it is,
$s[i,j]=\sum_{m=0}^{2}\sum_{n=0}^{2} I[i+m,\,j+n]\,K[m,n]$.

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-57.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10#57
lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-57.text: The textbook convolution: rotate the kernel by $180^\circ$ first.

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-58.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10#58
lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-58.text:
Should the kernel be flipped or not? How is this
sliding multiply-and-add written exactly?

lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-59.name: fig:lec06-kp03-p10#59
lec06kp03-u01-p10-nf-lec06-kp03-p10-59.text: Flipping the kernel changes the sign of the response of $K_{\mathrm h}$ ($-6$ becomes $6$); KP04 gives the exact definition.

lec06kp03-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge

steps.label: Layer stages
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate. Made from the confirmed lecture lec06-kp03: the pages were planned first, each page is mainly one native infographic, and terms are defined on the page where they are used. 11 main pages, plus 2 extension pages (other choices, exercises) that are not timed. Content marked Added is not in the course source and was added by the lecture. The exercise page gives hints only, no answers.

steps.label: Overview
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP03. Three prerequisites: the kernel and feature map of KP01, the activation functions of Week 2, and the backpropagation and gradient descent of Week 3. The sliding multiply-and-add of KP01 is only the first stage of a convolutional layer. A complete layer has three stages in order. Stage one is the convolution stage: the kernel slides over the input and multiplies and adds at each position, giving the feature map. Stage two is the detector stage: an activation function is applied to every cell of the feature map, deciding how strongly that position lights up. Stage three is the pooling stage: the map is cut into small blocks and each keeps one summary number, so the map becomes smaller. Think of the find-edges filter of a photo editor: apply the filter, keep only the positive responses, shrink the result. This unit answers two questions: what happens inside one layer, and where the nine numbers of the kernel come from. We start with what the kernel of stage one looks like. Next, the next page covers the two Prewitt kernels.

steps.label: Prewitt kernels
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the overview of the three stages. An edge is a place in an image where the brightness changes suddenly. Before deep learning became popular, image-processing engineers designed kernels by hand to find edges; the classic example is the pair of 3 by 3 Prewitt kernels. The horizontal kernel on the left has a top row of ones, a middle row of zeros and a bottom row of minus ones, so it computes the top row minus the bottom row; its response is largest on a horizontal edge, where top and bottom differ in brightness. The vertical kernel on the right computes the left column minus the right column and responds most to a vertical edge. Blue is plus one, red is minus one, grey is zero. On the next page we lay them on a small patch and compute. Next, the next page covers the patch example.

steps.label: Patch example
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the two Prewitt kernels. Take a 3 by 3 patch and call it X: its rows are 0, 1 and 2, dark on top and bright below. The kernel is as large as the patch, so it is laid down once. Horizontal kernel: row 0 times one adds up to 0; row 1 is multiplied by 0; row 2 has three twos times minus one, which is minus 6; the total is minus 6. Vertical kernel: every row gives one times v plus zero times v plus minus one times v, which is 0, so the total is 0. Transpose X, swapping rows and columns, and it becomes dark on the left and bright on the right; the two responses swap. The four boxes on the right show these four results; a red box marks a negative response. So a kernel really picks out the kind of edge it knows: a large absolute value means an edge in that direction, and the sign tells which side is brighter, a point the lecture added. The horizontal kernel is positive when the top is brighter and negative when the bottom is brighter, like the minus 6 of X. One patch gives one number; next, a whole image goes through stage one. Next, the next page covers stage one, convolution.

steps.label: Stage one
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the patch example. The main example was added by the lecture: a 6 by 6 image whose rows 1 to 3 and columns 0 to 3 form a bright block of brightness 2, the orange block; everything else is 0. The block has a top edge and a bottom edge. Take the valid output of KP01 with the horizontal kernel: each direction has 6 minus 3 plus 1, that is 4 positions, so the feature map is 4 by 4. Look at three representative cells. The red frame, s at 0, 0: the window covers rows 0 to 2; the top row is all 0 and the bottom row all 2, so 0 minus 2 times 3 is minus 6: the top edge, dark above bright. The green frame, s at 2, 0: rows 2 to 4; the top row is all 2 and the bottom row all 0, so plus 6: the bottom edge, bright above dark. The dashed violet frame, s at 0, 3: columns 3 to 5, and only column 3 of the bottom row is 2, so minus 2; the window covers only a small part of the block, so the response is smaller. Row 1 of the map is all 0: its windows cover rows 1 to 3, whose top and bottom rows are identical, so they give 0. Green cells are positive and red negative. Next, stage two decides what happens to the negative numbers. Next, the next page covers stage two, the detector.

steps.label: Stage two
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on stage one, convolution. Stage two is the detector: an activation function is applied to every cell of the feature map. Here it is the ReLU of Week 2, which turns a into the larger of 0 and a: negative numbers become 0 and positive numbers stay. Written out, r is this function applied to s. Look at the feature map on the left: row 0, in the dashed red frame, minus 6, minus 6, minus 4 and minus 2, all become 0; the other cells were not negative, so they stay. Only the bottom edge, bright above dark, is still lit; the top edge is wiped out. A common error here, added by the lecture: looking only at the size of the output of the horizontal kernel and forgetting its sign. An edge that is dark above bright gives a negative number and disappears after the ReLU; that is how the top edge vanished here. Next, stage three shrinks the map. Next, the next page covers stage three, pooling.

steps.label: Stage three
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on stage two, the detector. Stage three uses max pooling: cut the 4 by 4 map r into four non-overlapping 2 by 2 blocks, along the orange lines, and keep only the largest number of each block. The formula says y at u, v is the maximum of the four numbers of that block. The top-left and top-right blocks are all 0, so row 0 of y is 0, 0. The bottom-left block is four sixes and gives 6; the bottom-right block is 4, 2, 4, 2 and gives 4. So y has the rows 0, 0 and 6, 4. The image went from 6 by 6, to a 4 by 4 feature map, to a 2 by 2 pooled map. How to read 6 and 4: the bottom edge of the block lies in the lower half. The windows of the left half lie entirely on the bottom edge, so 6; those of the right half cover only part of it, so 4. Sixteen numbers shrink to four summaries, and the edge can still be located. Next: why is each of the three stages needed? Next, the next page covers why each stage is needed.

steps.label: All three
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on stage three, pooling. The strip on top shows the sizes: the image is 6 by 6, convolution gives 4 by 4, the detector keeps the size, and pooling gives 2 by 2. Without the detector: convolution is only multiply-and-add, a linear operation. As Week 2 showed, any number of stacked linear operations is still one linear operation, and two convolutions stacked directly equal a single convolution; Exercise 3 lets you check this by hand. The activation function lets the network express nonlinear relations. Without pooling: the feature map is about as large as the input, so later layers have many numbers to process. Pooling shrinks the map and makes small shifts matter less; this stability is only approximate, and KP08 to KP09 work it out. Without convolution: we are back to the fully connected layer of KP01 and lose sparse connectivity and parameter sharing. A common error is to think a convolutional layer is a single multiplication; it has three stages. But the horizontal kernel finds only one kind of edge: for another task, are these nine numbers still right? Next, the next page covers learning the kernel.

steps.label: Learn the kernel
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on why each stage is needed. Different tasks and different data need different kernels. Real images contain slanted lines, textures, corners and patterns of fur, and hand-tuning nine numbers for every case is not practical. A convolutional neural network treats every number of the kernel as a learnable weight, decided by the data just like the weights of the fully connected layer of Week 2. On the left, the hand-set horizontal kernel has fixed numbers; following the arrow, the same nine cells become weights. How is it learned? Look at the flow below. Green is the forward pass: the kernel convolves, followed by the ReLU, pooling and the later layers, and finally the loss e is computed. Red is the backward pass: backpropagation from Week 3 computes the partial derivative of the loss with respect to each kernel weight, and gradient descent updates it, subtracting the learning rate times its partial derivative. The next page shows why this partial derivative can be computed. Next, the next page covers why the gradient is easy.

steps.label: The gradient
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on learning the kernel. It can, because the convolution stage is linear in the kernel; this derivation was added by the lecture. Expand s at 2, 0 of the main example: it is I at 2, 0 times K at 0, 0, plus I at 2, 1 times K at 0, 1, and so on up to I at 4, 2 times K at 2, 2. Each kernel weight multiplies exactly one pixel, so the partial derivative of s with respect to a kernel weight is the pixel it multiplies. On the left, the green frame is the window of s at 2, 0 and the yellow box is its top-left pixel, I at 2, 0, whose value is 2; so the partial derivative of s at 2, 0 with respect to K at 0, 0 is 2. A partial derivative is the rate of change of the output when only one variable moves, from Week 3. The same kernel weight is used at every position, and backpropagation adds up the contributions of all positions with the chain rule of Week 3. A learned kernel may catch edges like Prewitt does, or textures, spots and more complex local patterns; a convolutional network does not invent a magical filter, it lets backpropagation replace hand-tuning. A common error is to think a convolutional network can only use edge kernels like Prewitt; Prewitt is just an example from the era of hand-tuning. One question is left. Next, the next page covers the question left for KP04.

steps.label: For KP04
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on why the gradient is easy. The formula of this unit follows KP01 and lays the kernel down as it is. The textbook convolution, however, rotates the kernel by 180 degrees first. This page is an observation added by the lecture. On the left is the horizontal kernel; rotated by 180 degrees, its top row becomes minus ones and its bottom row ones, exactly its own negative. So on X the original kernel gives minus 6 and the rotated kernel gives 6: the response changes sign. Should the kernel be flipped or not? How is this sliding multiply-and-add written as an exact formula? KP04 answers that. First, let us put the three stages in one sentence. Next, the next page covers the summary and misconceptions.

steps.label: Summary
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the question left for KP04. In one sentence: a convolutional layer has three stages, convolution, where the kernel slides and multiplies and adds, the detector, an activation function on every cell, and pooling, one summary per block; the numbers of the kernel are not designed by hand but treated as weights and learned by backpropagation. The four cards on top are the formal definitions: the convolution formula, the detector taking the larger of 0 and s, 2 by 2 max pooling keeping each block's maximum, and the gradient-descent update of the kernel. Below are four common misconceptions. A convolutional layer is not a single multiplication; it has three stages. A convolutional network is not limited to Prewitt edge kernels; modern layers learn their kernels from data. A larger output of the horizontal kernel does not by itself mean a clearer edge: look at the absolute value, and a negative response becomes 0 after the ReLU. Two convolutions stacked directly cannot learn nonlinear patterns; without an activation in between they equal one. The main line ends here; the last two pages are extensions. Next, the next page covers the extension on other choices.

steps.label: Extension: choices
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the summary and misconceptions. This page is optional, and its content was added by the lecture. The three-stage skeleton stays, but what is used inside each stage can vary. The detector need not be a ReLU; other activation functions of Week 2 also work. Pooling need not take the maximum either; taking the average is also common, and KP08 compares kinds of pooling. A layer can also have several kernels, and a colour image has three colour channels; these are left to KP07. The ReLU and max pooling of this unit are only the most common pair of choices. The last page is the exercises. Next, the next page covers the extension exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the extension on other choices. Four exercises; the page gives only the questions and hints, so work them out yourself and then check against the lecture. Exercise 1: a patch with rows 2, 2 and 0; compute the responses of the horizontal and the vertical kernel and compare the sign with the minus 6 of X; the hint is that the horizontal kernel is top minus bottom and the vertical one left minus right. Exercise 2 was added by the lecture: a 4 by 4 feature map; apply the ReLU, then 2 by 2 max pooling; the hint is to replace negative numbers by 0 first, then take each block's maximum. Exercise 3 was also added: a 1-D signal goes through the kernel 1, 1 and then the kernel 1, minus 1; compare with a single three-cell kernel, and ask whether a ReLU in between changes the result; the hint is to write the 1-D formula first, and the first pass gives 4 numbers. Exercise 4: take the main example through the three stages with the vertical kernel and say which edge of the bright block lights up; the hint is that the vertical kernel is left minus right and the block's left edge touches the border of the image. That ends KP03; the next unit, KP04, writes the sliding multiply-and-add as an exact formula and answers whether the kernel is flipped.
